local.title: The Smith County jail
local.lead: The jail is the single largest line in Smith County’s General Fund — and it already runs one of the region’s best-known jail gardens.

facts.v: $32,878,761 for FY2026-27 — about 27 cents of every General Fund dollar, up from $30,987,936 the year before.
1,139: Central Jail 660, Low/Medium Risk 432, Courthouse 5th floor 47 — about $79 a bed a day.
The county has contracted with other Texas counties to house inmates beyond its capacity, to stay in compliance with state jail standards (Docket #12).

Jail inmates run a garden on Highway 155 and give all of the produce to the East Texas Food Bank — in excess of 160,000 pounds, the food bank’s CEO estimated. The sheriff says people line up wanting to work in it.
Not on the Texas Commission on Jail Standards’ list of non-compliant jails as of Sept 26, 2026.
No education or trade-credential program inside the jail was found documented on a primary source (Docket #11).

proposals.title: Turn the garden into a credential
proposals.summary: The garden already works and people ask to join it. Add what makes it last: a Tyler Junior College certificate in horticulture, food safety, or equipment operation, earned in the garden and the kitchen and continued after release.
proposals.why_here: At $32.9 million a year, even a small drop in people coming back is real money — and the county’s own college is right here.
proposals.first_step: Ask the sheriff and commissioners court to pilot one short certificate with Tyler Junior College for garden and kitchen crews, tracked by who comes back and who gets hired.

ask.label: Weigh in on the open question

proposals.title: An offered work crew that builds homes
proposals.summary: Every morning the crew is offered: wake up, eat, and go build — or stay in the cell. Crew members earn pay and real credentials working alongside a licensed builder on homes for local families, through a partner like Habitat for Humanity or a community land trust. Some will stick with it after release; either way, the community gets stronger.
math: depends on who is eligible and chooses it
Labor per modest 1,200 sq ft house (trainee crew, ordinary construction)
Houses a year the crew could build
scales with the crew — dozens a year are possible if funded
limits: Labor isn’t the limit — money is. At the national average of about $162 a square foot, a 1,200 sq ft house costs roughly $190,000 to build; materials, licensed electricians and plumbers, permits, and land still need funding.
Most people are held for weeks, so the crew is always partly new; it needs paid, trained crew leads — often people who stayed on after release.
Houses given to families work best through a nonprofit or land trust; what a county itself may give away is a question for a lawyer.

proposals.title: A door you can walk in
proposals.summary: Some people know they need structure before a crime ever happens. Offer a voluntary live-in program — housing, work, training, recovery — that a person can choose to enter and is free to leave. Choosing structure without a record is honor preserved.
limits: Nobody can be locked up without a crime or a court order, so it must stay a door that opens both ways.
“Voluntary” can be bent by desperation or a judge’s pressure; the design must guard against both.
Residents’ work must be paid and for their own growth — never unpaid labor for a company.
